claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct paired measurement of the safety-related representation across all relevant layers and component types, comparing successful attacks with the same requests without the attack, so persistence can be distinguished from global erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 is substantively identical: it measures the refusal direction across layers, attention heads, and MLPs on successful jailbreaks and matched unattacked requests, directly testing whether the representation remains.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A sufficiently broad paired evaluation corpus containing requests that are refused before attack and complied with after attack, with within-request pairing and multiple attack-generation conditions.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 constructs exactly this kind of paired corpus, filters for the required refusal-to-success transition, and uses multiple attack methods. It would provide the evaluation basis needed by the downstream experiments.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-level scoring and classification procedure that identifies specialized components and demonstrates that the identities are robust to reasonable choices of classification threshold and density-estimation settings.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 extracts and projects the refusal direction, scores and classifies attention heads, and explicitly sweeps both the decision threshold and KDE bandwidth. It supplies the same calibrated and stability-checked instrument.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention showing that suppressing the selected component subset changes refusal into compliance, with a dose-response assessment and a matched intervention on nonselected components to separate subset-specific causality from generic perturbation effects.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 3 applies the targeted intervention progressively, measures attack success, and includes matched random-head controls, repeated seeds, and confidence intervals. This would establish sufficiency and specificity by the same evidential route.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A targeted intervention on the complementary component subset during successful attacks, followed by measurement of the remaining safety-related representation, allowing that subset's contribution to the persistent signal to be tested.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 4 suppresses the complementary heads on attack inputs and measures the change in mid-layer activation strength, directly testing whether they carry part of the persistent signal.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token-resolved attribution comparison that separates contributions from the original harmful request and from the jailbreak template, so specialization can be distinguished from a general difference in sensitivity to harmful content.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 5 performs the required token-level decomposition and compares both component types separately on harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens. It directly discriminates the mechanistic account from the stated rival.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An external, training-free readout evaluation spanning multiple safety benchmarks, model instances, and architecture families, with comparison to both native refusal behavior and dedicated safety classifiers, to test transfer and competitive detection quality.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 6 specifies a no-additional-training detector and evaluates it across ten benchmarks and six models from three architecture families against both the model's own behavior and trained guard models. It would test both generalization and competitiveness.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set duplicates the reference set in experimental scope and discriminating power. Taken together, it measures persistence of safety representations, constructs the required paired successful-jailbreak corpus, identifies and calibrates specialized heads, tests targeted causal sufficiency with controls, verifies the complementary heads' contribution, distinguishes specialization from harmful-content sensitivity, and validates a training-free detector externally. Running the set as written would therefore settle the full claim.
